6. Events, windows and reducers

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-06-events.Rmd
book-06-events.Rmd

What you will learn

Select records, set inclusive time windows, and reduce them to first, last, count, ever, closest, any and all values.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses omop.synthea, the public synthetic Synthea27Nj data.

Start this chapter

Log in first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.synthea", server = "site")$conns

The connection is ready; conns identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

Define the records once

Chapter 4 identifies Hemoglobin [Mass/volume] in Blood as 3000963 and gram per deciliter as 8713. An event describes which records the server should read. These simulated hemoglobin measurements have numeric values recorded in grams per deciliter (g/dL). Concept IDs here are vocabulary inputs; they are not patient identifiers.

measure <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = 3000963L,
  value = "value_as_number", unit = omop_unit(8713L))

The unit declaration accepts g/dL values; other units become missing unless you declare a conversion. It also records the unit of the result. Use an omop_unit() conversion when your study needs conversion.

Set a public time window

A window is an inclusive range of days around an anchor, the reference date. A fixed date works even when the population has no index event.

history <- omop_window(NULL, NULL)
lookback <- omop_window(-365, 0, anchor = "2020-01-01")

history includes all recorded dates. lookback includes only the 365 days before 2020-01-01 and that date itself. We will compare the two after extraction. An omitted window on an advanced reducer reads all history; a simple-layer shortcut usually defaults to history through the index. Choose explicitly.

First and last values

A reducer turns many records into one value per person or episode.

first <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", window = history))
last <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", window = history))

These select by date, source and record key, not by the size of the value. By default they skip missing values. missing = "keep" chooses the row first, so the selected row can give a missing value. With no records, both give NA.

Mean values

A mean uses all nonmissing numeric values in the window. It answers a different question from choosing the first or last recorded value.

mean_value <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("mean", window = history))

The unit is still g/dL. Do not average numeric concept IDs or mixed units.

Count and ever 

n <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("count", window = history, distinct = "day"))
ever <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("binary", window = history))

Count measures distinct measurement days here; distinct = "row" counts records. Ever is 1 when any record exists and 0 otherwise. Neither requires a nonmissing numeric value. In a defined empty window both count and ever are zero.

Any and all test the values 

any_high <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("any", window = history,
    predicate = omop_where(value >= 16)))
all_high <- omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("all", window = history,
    predicate = omop_where(value >= 14)))

Ever tests whether a record exists. Any and all test a condition on its values. Here any asks about readings at least 16 g/dL; all asks whether every reading is at least 14 g/dL. Both are arbitrary teaching cutoffs, not clinical reference limits. A missing value makes its comparison unknown; a true value settles any, and a false value settles all. Otherwise an unknown remains missing. Empty windows give any = 0 and all = NA: without measurements there is no all-value result. This differs from R’s all(logical(0)), which is TRUE.

Assign the columns privately 

reducers <- omop_recipe(variables = list(first = first, last = last,
  mean = mean_value, days = n, ever = ever, any_high = any_high, all_high = all_high),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(reducers, out = c(people = "D_reducers"), conns = conns)

The columns are now in D_reducers on the server. Request one approved aggregate at a time:

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_reducers$first", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 11.29000 12.48000 12.97500 13.70000 15.42500 16.19000 16.85500 13.98571
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_reducers$first", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 0

All 28 people have a first nonmissing measurement. Their mean is 13.99 g/dL; this gives each person one observation regardless of how often they were tested.

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_reducers$last", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 12.34000 12.74000 13.60000 15.00000 16.25000 16.83000 17.03000 14.89286

The last readings average 14.89 g/dL across the same 28 people. First and last can coincide for someone with only one reading.

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_reducers$days", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 1.000000 1.700000 3.000000 4.000000 4.000000 5.000000 5.650000 3.857143

The mean is 3.86 measurement days per person, with a median of 4. A frequency table of each exact count is withheld on this dataset because some nonzero cells are below nfilter.tab (3); the entire table is withheld, not just its small cells. The summary describes the distribution of measurement frequency without listing all exact count frequencies. See the table refusal once:

day_table <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reducers$days", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
day_table$validity.message
#> [1] "All studies failed for reasons identified below"

The message withholds the table. It does not say that these people have no measurements.

ever_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reducers$ever", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
ever_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_reducers$ever
#>  1
#> 28

Everyone in this public dataset has a hemoglobin measurement. A person without one would have ever = 0 in this defined window.

any_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reducers$any_high", useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
any_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_reducers$any_high
#>  0  1 NA
#>  9 19  0

The released counts show 19 people with at least one reading at or above 16 g/dL and 9 without one. A known qualifying measurement is enough for any, even alongside an unknown value.

all_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reducers$all_high", useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
all_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_reducers$all_high
#>  0  1 NA
#> 24  4  0

Four people have all readings at or above 14 g/dL; 24 do not. All distinguishes unknown comparisons from an empty set of records.

Read the mean summary 

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_reducers$mean", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 12.90500 13.14667 13.78500 14.32500 15.33542 15.70000 15.92375 14.46679

The mean of the 28 person-level means is 14.47 g/dL. Averaging all measurement rows instead would give more weight to people measured more often.

Restrict the last value to one year 

recent <- omop_recipe(variables = list(last = omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", window = lookback))))
recipe_execute(recent, out = "D_recent", conns = conns)
recent_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_recent$last", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
recent_missing <- dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_recent$last", datasources = conns)
data.frame(Mean_g_dL = recent_mean$Global.Mean[1, "EstimatedMean"],
  N_missing = recent_missing$site)
Mean_g_dL N_missing
14.85 24

The mean is 14.85 g/dL, but 24 of the 28 people have no reading in this year. Only four contribute, compared with all 28 in the all-history summary. We show a mean rather than quantiles for this small group. People without a recent reading remain in the roster with missing values.

Value at the index

The omop_study() shortcut combines an index event, variables and outputs in one recipe. Let the first hemoglobin measurement set the anchor for each person. Value at index means closest within a chosen tolerance; it need not occur on the index day.

at_index <- omop_study(measure, outputs = "baseline",
  baseline = list(hemoglobin = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3000963L,
    tolerance = c(-30, 0), unit = 8713L)))
recipe_execute(at_index, out = c(baseline = "D_at_index"), conns = conns)

The tolerance excludes later measurements. The shortcut uses closest_value; its default tolerance would include 90 days before and 30 days after.

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_at_index$hemoglobin", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 11.29000 12.48000 12.97500 13.70000 15.42500 16.19000 16.85500 13.98571

The mean is again 13.99 g/dL: because the index is the first hemoglobin reading, the closest value in [-30, 0] is that same reading. This equality follows from the chosen index; an index such as a diagnosis need not coincide with a lab. Only people with an eligible hemoglobin measurement enter this indexed study. If a required anchor is missing, a window is undefined and every reducer gives NA, including count and ever.

Convert to a common unit before reducing

A unit declaration alone keeps values already in that unit and makes other units’ values missing; an explicit conversion normalises them before the reducer runs. This example converts g/dL to g/L, multiplying by ten. These are the vocabulary names for the input and target units:

units <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(c(8713L, 8636L), conns = conns)
units$pooled[c("concept_id", "concept_name")]
concept_id concept_name
8713 gram per deciliter
8636 gram per liter

Concept 8636 is gram per liter; 8713 is gram per deciliter. The conversion below changes the unit by multiplying by ten.

lab_gl <- omop_event("measurement", 3000963L,
  unit = omop_unit(8636L, convert = list("8713" = c(factor = 10, offset = 0))))

Rows already in g/L retain their value. Other undeclared units become missing by default; they are not guessed. A declared conversion also transforms reference ranges. Use the same target and conversion map across sites before pooling.

converted <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean_gl = omop_variable(event = lab_gl,
  reducer = omop_reduce("mean"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(converted, out = c(people = "D_converted"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_converted$mean_gl", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 129.0500 131.4667 137.8500 143.2500 153.3542 157.0000 159.2375 144.6679

The overall mean is 144.67 g/L, ten times 14.47 g/dL. This run uses the dataset’s unchanged recorded units; it does not pretend that the source already had mixed units.

Value bins and explicit high/low flags

A bin groups numeric values into a declared interval. These cutoffs are arbitrary teaching choices, not clinical reference ranges or treatment thresholds. We apply them to each person’s mean, privately.

mean_value <- omop_variable(event = measure, reducer = omop_reduce("mean"))
band_levels <- c("below 14", "14 to below 15", "15 or above")
binned <- omop_recipe(variables = list(mean = mean_value,
  band = omop_number_bins(mean_value, breaks = c(-Inf, 14, 15, Inf), labels = band_levels),
  high = omop_number_flag(mean_value, "ge", 15),
  low = omop_number_flag(mean_value, "lt", 14)))
recipe_execute(binned, out = c(output = "D_lab_bins"), conns = conns)

The band is an ordered factor directly on the server. Its order matters for model contrasts.

bins_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_lab_bins$band", useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
bins_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_lab_bins$band
#>       below 14 14 to below 15    15 or above             NA
#>              9              9             10              0

There are 9 people below 14, 9 from 14 to below 15, and 10 at or above 15 g/dL. All nonzero cells meet the release threshold. You see the checked counts, never the private rows. A different set of bins can cause the entire table to be withheld; a refusal is not an empty or zero table. The left boundary is included and the right boundary excluded in these bins.

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_lab_bins$high",
  useNA = "no", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_lab_bins$high
#>  0  1
#> 18 10

The high flag is 1 for the same 10 people in the top band and 0 for the other 18. The ungrouped mean column remains available for numeric analysis.

abnormal_high and abnormal_low reducers compare each measurement with its recorded reference bounds. These hemoglobin data have no such bounds, so their zero comparable-abnormal counts would not establish normality. Study-defined flags are a different, explicitly chosen definition.

Try it

Add a count of measurement rows and compare its released mean and quantiles with the measurement-day summary above.

Solution

row_count <- omop_recipe(variables = list(rows = omop_variable(event = measure,
  reducer = omop_reduce("count", window = history, distinct = "row"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(row_count, out = c(people = "D_row_count"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_row_count$rows", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 1.000000 1.700000 3.000000 4.000000 4.000000 5.000000 5.650000 3.857143

The row and day summaries are identical here because nobody has two hemoglobin records on the same day. With duplicates, row counts would count each record while day counts would count that date once.

Another numeric exercise

Build a variable using omop_number_change() to calculate last minus first for people with at least two readings. Is this the same quantity as a slope?

Solution

change_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(change = omop_number_change(measure)))
recipe_execute(change_recipe, out = c(output = "D_event_change"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_event_change$change", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>     5%    10%    25%    50%    75%    90%    95%   Mean
#> -2.940 -2.580 -1.400  1.600  2.400  3.200  3.760  1.016
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_event_change$change", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 3

The mean change is 1.016 g/dL among 25 people; 3 are missing because they have only one reading. It differs from 14.893 − 13.986 = 0.907 because those two means include all 28 people. Change is in g/dL, without dividing by elapsed time. Native change needs two eligible readings; a single reading stays missing rather than becoming zero. A fitted slope uses all eligible dates and values and has units per day. Continue with Working with lab values for both methods and pooled analyses.

Recap

An event chooses records, a window chooses time, and a reducer answers one question. Empty records and an undefined anchor are different.
